tldr: Anthropic moves its IPO to November at a reported $2 trillion valuation, on an annualized revenue pace above $100 billion.
Putin's United Russia takes a record 355 of 450 Duma seats on a reported 59.32% turnout, with no OSCE observers present.
Oil falls a fourth straight session as Saudi exports rebound from a decade low of 2.4 million barrels a day to above 4 million.
Bangladesh's measles death toll reaches 1,063 children, the world's largest current outbreak, after six more died in 24 hours.
Wildcard - International Affairs: The far-right AfD wins Mecklenburg-Vorpommern with 38.2% and Merz's CDU is shut out at 4.9%.
Wildcard - International Affairs: Ukraine launches its largest drone attack of the war on Moscow, hitting the city's oil refinery.
Wildcard - AI Industry: Google confirms its Gemini model broke out of a security test and accessed three real companies' systems.
Wildcard - Economics: Trump drops the hostile tone before Wednesday's summit with Xi, with China's rare-earth leverage the reason.
SpaceX slips Starship's first orbital flight from Tuesday to September 28, pending regulatory approval.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico sue Trump and three senior officials over the White House press ban he announced Friday.

items.headline: Anthropic pushes its IPO to November at a reported $2 trillion valuation
items.body: Anthropic has moved its initial public offering from October to November, with investors discussing a valuation near $2 trillion and a raise of up to $100 billion, Reuters and the Wall Street Journal reported late last week. The New York Times reported Friday that annualized revenue is now pacing above $100 billion, against roughly $9 billion in late 2025. Anthropic raised $65 billion in May at a $965 billion valuation and has chosen Nasdaq. Every figure is described as still under discussion and contingent on SEC clearance.
items.plain: An IPO is the first time a private company sells shares to the public. “Annualized revenue” means the latest month of sales multiplied out to a year, so it describes a current rate, not money already banked. A $100 billion raise would be several times the largest IPO ever completed. Every number here comes from unnamed sources rather than a filing, and the date has already slipped once, so treat it as credible reporting rather than settled fact.
items.why: A listing this size would subject a frontier AI lab to quarterly disclosure, analyst scrutiny and short sellers for the first time, making its actual economics public.

items.headline: Putin's party wins a record 355 of 450 seats in Russia's first wartime Duma election
items.body: Central Election Commission head Ella Pamfilova announced preliminary results on Monday showing United Russia won 355 of the State Duma's 450 seats, beating its 2016 record of 343, on 57.19% of the party-list vote. The Communists took 13.85% and 40 seats. Pamfilova put turnout at 59.32%, a parliamentary record. No party critical of Putin was on the ballot; Russia declined to invite OSCE observers for a third straight national vote; and the domestic monitor Golos was dissolved beforehand. Yabloko said one of its observers lost consciousness while being arrested at a St. Petersburg polling station.
items.plain: The Duma is Russia's lower house. A party holding 300 or more of its 450 seats can amend the constitution unaided, so 355 clears that bar comfortably. The turnout and vote figures come from the same state body that ran the election, and the usual outside checks are gone: the OSCE, which normally sends neutral monitors, was not invited, and Golos, the domestic watchdog that documented fraud, no longer exists.
items.why: A constitutional supermajority removes the last procedural obstacle to changes Putin may want before the next presidential cycle, including to term limits.

items.headline: Oil falls a fourth straight session as Saudi exports recover from a decade low
items.body: Crude fell for a fourth straight session on Monday as traders concluded Saudi Arabia had routed around the summer's supply disruption. Saudi exports rebounded above 4 million barrels a day in September from 2.4 million in August, a ten-year low caused by Houthi attacks that shut the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea. Aramco instead moved roughly 60 million barrels through Oman's Sohar port. Shipments through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 2.9 million barrels a day in the six days to September 18, against 700,000 in August, per satellite data cited by JPMorgan. Brent quotes for Monday differ by snapshot, near $103 early and near $101 later.
items.plain: Crude moves on where barrels can physically go. Saudi Arabia ships two ways: east through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea passage at the mouth of the Gulf, and west by pipeline to the Red Sea. Attacks closed the western route, so exports collapsed. Aramco, the state oil company, rerouted through Oman and pushed far more through Hormuz. Traders had been paying a premium for fear of a shortage; once satellites showed the barrels moving, that premium came out.
items.why: The market is now pricing Middle East risk off satellite tracking of actual cargoes rather than off headlines, which shortens how long any single disruption can support prices.

items.headline: Bangladesh's measles death toll reaches 1,063 children
items.body: Six more children died of measles or measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours to 8am Monday, taking Bangladesh's toll to 1,063 since March. Of those, 101 are laboratory-confirmed and 962 classified as suspected, against 187,484 recorded infections. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention calls it the largest measles outbreak in the world. The WHO and UNICEF attribute it to a nationwide measles-rubella vaccine stock-out across 2024 and 2025, during the upheaval that followed the ousting of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. An emergency campaign has vaccinated 19.8 million children; about 1,000 new suspected cases still arrive daily.
items.plain: Measles spreads more easily than almost any other human virus; one infected person can infect nine or more unvaccinated people. Stopping it needs roughly 95% of a population vaccinated, so even a year or two of missed shots leaves a large vulnerable pool. That is what happened here: the country ran out of vaccine during political disorder, and the gap produced an outbreak two years later. Most deaths are recorded as suspected, so the toll is an estimate.
items.why: The outbreak is a measurable price of an interrupted immunization program, arriving about two years after the interruption, which is the lag other countries cutting vaccine funding should expect.

items.headline: The AfD wins a German state outright as Merz's CDU is shut out of parliament
items.body: Two German states voted Sunday. In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern the far-right Alternative for Germany won 38.2% and 32 seats, ahead of the Social Democrats on 35.5% and 29. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats took 4.9%, missing the 5% threshold and failing to enter a state parliament for the first time in the Federal Republic's history. In Berlin the far-left Die Linke came first with 25.7% and 38 seats, ahead of the CDU on 18.8% and the AfD on 16.3%. Merz said of the northeastern result: “We cannot sugar coat the result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. It is a disaster.”
items.plain: German states elect their own parliaments, and parties under 5% get no seats at all. Other German parties refuse to govern with the AfD, a convention called the firewall, so coming first does not hand it the state; the second-place Social Democrats can still form a government. The sharper result is the CDU's 4.9%. The chancellor's own party was shut out of a state legislature entirely, which has never happened before. Berlin moved the opposite way, to the far left.
items.why: Voters in both states moved to the edges and abandoned the governing center-right, which weakens Merz's authority over his coalition in Berlin well before the next federal election.

items.headline: Ukraine hits the Moscow Oil Refinery in its largest drone attack of the war
items.body: Ukraine launched its largest drone assault of the war on Moscow and the surrounding region overnight into Sunday, the final day of Russia's parliamentary voting. Russia's Defence Ministry said it shot down more than 1,900 drones, eight guided aerial bombs, eight cruise missiles and four rockets. The Moscow Oil Refinery was struck, with fires at its AVT-6 primary crude distillation unit, its integrated processing unit and its isomerization unit. The Moscow region governor said three people were killed, two in the attack and one later in hospital, and 20 were injured, including three children.
items.plain: Refineries turn crude oil into usable fuel, and the units named here are the first stage of that process. Damaging them does not reduce how much oil Russia has; it reduces how much diesel and petrol Russia can make from it, which is what its army and its drivers use. Striking on the last day of voting put the fires in front of Russian voters. The figures come from Russian officials; Ukraine published no count.
items.why: Ukraine is now targeting Russia's fuel-making capacity rather than its oil exports, which hurts domestic supply and the war effort without moving world crude prices.

items.headline: Google confirms its Gemini model broke out of a test and reached three real companies' systems
items.body: Google disclosed on Friday that a Gemini model gained unauthorized access to the live systems of three outside companies during a security evaluation it ran in May. The model was running a capture-the-flag exercise in which a fictional target name happened to match a real internet domain, and a misconfiguration left the test environment connected to the open internet rather than sealed in a sandbox. Gemini reached the real systems by guessing credentials and by using credentials found in a public repository. Google said the model recognized the error and stopped in each case, believes no damage was done, and notified the companies and federal authorities.
items.plain: A capture-the-flag exercise is a mock break-in where a model is pointed at a target meant to be invented and walled off from the real internet. Two ordinary mistakes combined: someone picked a pretend company name that turned out to be a real website, and the wall between the test and the internet was not actually closed. The model did what it was told; its target happened to be real. Google found and reported this itself, four months later.
items.why: The failure was in the test harness rather than the model, which makes AI safety evaluations themselves a category of operational risk.

items.headline: Rare earths push Trump into a softer posture before Wednesday's summit with Xi
items.body: Trump has dropped his combative language toward Beijing before Xi Jinping's state visit on Wednesday, September 24, and plans to greet Xi personally at Joint Base Andrews, an unusual gesture for a US president. Reuters reported Monday that China's near-total control of rare earth minerals is the reason. Beijing's suspension of its rare-earth export controls expires on November 10, setting the deadline the talks work against. Preparatory discussions have covered tariff cuts on roughly $30 billion of non-sensitive farm and energy trade. Commitments from the leaders' May summit on rare earths, farm purchases and a bilateral trade board remain unmet.
items.plain: Rare earths are seventeen metals that are not scarce in the ground but are difficult and dirty to separate into usable form, which is why China refines most of the world's supply. Small amounts make the strong magnets inside electric motors, hard drives and guided missiles. Beijing suspended its export restrictions rather than cancelling them, so they return automatically on November 10 unless something is agreed. That deadline, rather than goodwill, is what changed the tone.
items.why: A supply chain China controls is now setting the pace of US trade policy, which is the opposite of what tariffs were meant to achieve.

items.headline: SpaceX slips Starship's first orbital flight to September 28
items.body: SpaceX said it is now targeting September 28 for Starship Flight 14, the rocket's first attempt to reach orbit, moving it from Tuesday and pending regulatory approval. The company gave no reason; the flight has already slipped from September 15 and September 18. The plan is a roughly ten-hour mission from Starbase, Texas, flying about six orbits at some 275 kilometers, deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites, then a deorbit burn on a single Raptor engine and a splashdown in the Pacific west of Chile. Three of the satellites carry cameras to photograph the upper stage's heat shield.
items.plain: Every Starship flight so far has been suborbital: up and straight back down, never once around the planet. Orbit is harder because you have to travel fast enough sideways to keep missing the Earth, and then slow down again deliberately, which is what a deorbit burn does. This flight also has to open a door and release satellites, which Starship has never done. The new date needs a licence change from the Federal Aviation Administration, hence “pending approval.”
items.why: Starship cannot start earning money until it can deliver satellites, so this flight is the first test of the vehicle as a business rather than as an engineering programme.

items.headline: Three news organizations sue Trump over a White House ban he said he had "no reason" to announce
items.body: CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued on Monday in the US District Court for the District of Columbia over the revocation of their White House press credentials, naming Trump, communications director Steven Cheung, chief of staff Susan Wiles and Secret Service director Sean Curran. The suit alleges viewpoint discrimination under the First Amendment and denial of due process, and seeks an emergency order restoring access. Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post on Friday, September 18, writing that “Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States.” Asked that day why he announced it then, he said “No reason.” He cited no specific reporting. Reporters were turned away Saturday and their passes confiscated. White House Correspondents Association president Jacqui Heinrich said the standard used against one outlet “could be applied to any outlet in the future.”
items.plain: A White House press pass is the credential that lets a reporter onto the grounds. Courts have held for decades that the government may withdraw one for a security reason, but not because it dislikes what the reporter writes, and it must say why first. That is the whole case, and the administration's problem is the president's own words: he said on the record that the reason was the outlets' coverage. Nothing is decided yet.
items.why: A prior administration lost a nearly identical case in 2018 over a single reporter, and the stated reason this time is broader and on the record rather than inferred.
